paper.title: Computing Partial Recursive Functions by Deterministic Symport/Antiport P-Systems
paper.abstract: In this paper, we prove that deterministic 1-membrane systems with symport/antiport rules are Turing-complete. Our proof is based on the notion of numerical partial recursive function computed by numerical programs of a language with simple instructions, defined by Martin Davis and Elaine Weyuker [10]. We reduced the task from partial recursive functions to numerical programs and then to symport/antiport P systems.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.NO_LIMITATIONS: No limitations section and no inline acknowledgment of constraints. The conclusion restates the result and names future work only; the paper does not discuss that computational completeness of symport/antiport systems with one membrane was already known, nor the cost (number of objects and rules per instruction, steps per simulated instruction) of the construction.

verdict.summary: Computability-theory paper proving Turing completeness of deterministic one-membrane symport/antiport P systems by simulating Davis-Sigal-Weyuker numerical programs. Formalism is native to the subject and proportionate; the proof is a standard instruction-by-instruction simulation argued somewhat loosely, the result restates known universality without positioning against prior symport/antiport universality results, and no limitations are discussed.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Proof that deterministic 1-membrane symport/antiport P systems with an input membrane compute all partial recursive functions, via a reduction from the numerical programs of Davis, Sigal and Weyuker (increment, decrement, conditional jump) to symport/antiport rules.
**Level:** 5 (Very High)
**Rationale:** The paper's sole contribution is a computational-universality (Turing-completeness) result, which the classification rules place at Level 5. The construction itself is the well-known register-machine simulation idea (the paper says so: "this idea was already used many times in membrane computing"), so the novelty is modest, but the concept class is a universality proof and the formal apparatus is the subject matter.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 10 numbered (3.1-3.3 composition, primitive recursion, unbounded minimisation; 4.1-4.7 the P-system construct, initial configuration, configuration of order k, halting computation, computing P system, valid system, computed function), plus unnumbered preliminaries on multisets and program semantics
- Theorems: 1 (Theorem 5.1)
- Proofs: 1 (induction on snapshots)
- Equations: numerous set-builder, tuple and functional definitions; one algorithm (ConstructRules, Fig. 2); several program listings and macro expansions

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 10 x 2 + 1 x 3 + 1 x 4 = 27
Expected range (Level 5): 60-150
Ratio: 0.18x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. Multiset notation, tuple definitions of P systems, and the formal semantics of snapshots are the standard language of membrane computing and computability; they are needed to state the simulation precisely and are used in the proof. Set notation here (multiset union M_im ∪ m, alphabets Γ \ Σ) is the subject matter, not a stand-in for list operations.

### Issues
- Definition 4.3 (configuration of order k) and the Section 3 constructions for composition, primitive recursion and minimisation are textbook material reproduced at length; the reduction from partial recursive functions to numerical programs is not new and could have been cited from [10].
- The induction step is only gestured at ("the proof is similar as for the basis case"), and determinism is asserted ("We can easily see that ... the next configuration is unique") rather than argued against the rule set in Fig. 2.
- Errors in the text: Definition 4.6 states "Output(C1) = Output(C1)" (should be C2); the minimisation program skips label L_{n'+4}; the composition program refers to "Y ← g_i" where f is meant.
- No instructions addressed to an AI or reviewer were found in the text.

---

## Citation Analysis

Single author; none of the 11 references is by the author (SCR 0%). References are on-topic (Păun's introduction and handbook, the symport/antiport origin paper, Romero-Jiménez and Pérez-Jiménez on computing partial recursive functions with transition P systems, Davis-Sigal-Weyuker). Notably absent is the prior literature establishing universality of symport/antiport systems with few membranes, against which the claim of novelty should have been positioned. No citation-manipulation patterns.

---

## Structural Analysis

The central claim (Theorem 5.1 and the resulting Turing completeness) is supported by a constructive proof; the motivational claim that the approach offers "clues about how classical programs written in the assembly languages ... could be directly translated to hypothetical membrane system processors" is asserted without support. No limitations are acknowledged, and the related-work section discusses only three papers on different P-system variants. As a pure theory paper there is nothing to release; no artifact is linked or claimed.

---

## Conclusion

A short, competent computability paper whose formalism is entirely appropriate to a universality result and well within the Level 5 range. Its weaknesses are scholarly rather than formal: the result is close to known universality theorems for symport/antiport systems and is not positioned against them, the inductive proof is sketched, several typographical errors affect definitions, and no limitations are stated.
